concepts.hook: Hesk ties one knot into the Reel-cord each time the Sun-Kite turns over a moon, and the stars are the knots she has tied since Aun cut the string.
*Olun* — "the Needle-Mother" — sewed the first sailcloth on the midwinter, and her stitches stayed up in the sky when the cloth below wore through.
Ennu's first Sun-Kite tail frayed in a spring gale and was patched with goat-hair, and the patches still show as a row of dim stars along the road.
*Hani* — "the Wool-Cutter" — cut the spring fleece so fast that her blade threw sparks, and the sparks are the stars still falling off the goats' backs.
*Kestu*, lowered on a line down the cliff to take gull eggs in early summer, felt the rope go slack and was never hauled up, so she hangs on the road still.
*Skelra* — "the Split Oar" — is the boat-oar that cracked on the midsummer crossing and was lashed with wet hide, and it still rows the Lamp Road.
Aun flew a second kite along the road after the cut, looking for the place where the string had gone, and it has not yet come down.
Sil carried a lamp up the road to search for Aun and set it down at the crossing to rest her hands, and it still burns where she left it.
Islanders crossing the winter strait roped together with a lamp at every belt, so no one walking in the snow could drift off alone.
The Gale took a fisherman's hat on the first morning of spring and he chased it up the road, and the hat is still just out of his reach.
*Mirrek* cut the birth-cords through the midwinter nights, and the stars are the knots she tied in them before each cut.
The fire kept through the longest night of the year was lit from a single spark of Aun's knife, and the islanders still carry its light to their hearths.
*Tamun* cut her dead husband's shawl into a sail for the boat that will fetch him back from the Upper Sea, and she is still stitching it.
*Ruvan* scratched every gull egg of the harvest onto a bone with a hot nail, and the tally is still short by one, which the Gulls keep looking for.
*Oreth* waited through the whole summer for the sun to dry the brine in her shallow pans, and her pans are the bright square stars along the shore of the road.
Autumn fish were hung on poles to dry in the cold wind, and the stars lie in rows like split cod on the racks.
A keeper sat by the smokehouse fire every night of winter, and the small light at the door is her, still keeping the smoke going.
Mesket baked the harvest bread too hot and burned the first loaf black, and the Gulls carried it up the road as a dark star that nobody will eat.
The bell on the lead goat rang through every spring kidding, and its stars are the tinkling that the mothers still listen for in their sleep.
At midsummer the Sun-Kite line is staked to a grey stone on the shore, and the stone is the one bright point that never drifts along the road.

concepts.gloss: The Race to the Standing Stone
concepts.hook: Aun won the midsummer kite race to the standing stone by cutting the other kites' lines, and the losers are still racing him up the road.
*Varo* walked backward down the rope-walk, spinning the cord as she went, and the stars are the twist of that cord that she has not yet finished.
In spring the sea breaks the ice and a boat pushes through the floes with one long oar, a pale line of stars that marks where the ice gave way.
The goat chosen for the midsummer feast was marked with a red ribbon, and its horns are the two bright stars that turn toward the cooking fires.
The autumn net came up so full that the boat sank a hand's width, and the crew still hauls at it, shouting over the weight.
At midwinter men haul the Sun-Kite down from the road to mend it, and their rope is so stiff with frost that it rings when they pull.
At midsummer a couple is tied wrist to wrist with a kite-line and walks to the shore, and the line is the faint thread of stars between two lamps.
Tavo tore a curved piece from the Sun-Kite's edge in a spring gale, and the bent moon is the cloth he dropped, which the Sun-Kite is still missing.
Two fishers argued all night over when the tide would turn until it turned on its own, and they still argue, though the sea has long since settled it.
